summary: Shanghai Jiao Tong University authors add a knowledge-acquisition stage before repair. A Questioner, guided by a four-category template (mechanism and behavior, design and usage, locating and structure, ecosystem and standards), writes N=2 questions about the issue. Parallel, read-only Answerer agents explore the repository and write evidence-grounded answers. The QA pairs are prepended to an unchanged Mini-SWE-Agent resolver. On SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks), Pass@1 rises from 58.4 to 62.2 with GPT-5-mini and from 66.4 to 70.8 with DeepSeek-V3.2, above LocAgent, CoSIL, LingmaAgent and SWE-Debate, and cheaper than the latter two. A human audit finds 230 of 232 QA pairs factually supported. Replacing the QA with a single 'solution proposal' drops Pass@1 to 66.0, below no pre-repair stage at all.

claims.claim: ACQUIRE raises Pass@1 by up to 4.4 pp and outperforms all pre-repair methods on both models
claims.evidence: Table I: +3.8 (GPT-5-mini) and +4.4 (DeepSeek-V3.2); best baselines +1.6 and +2.4. One run per configuration. Per-instance flips are 44 fail-to-pass vs 22 pass-to-fail (§V-B1); a sign test on those counts gives roughly p = 0.007. The 1-2 pp gaps to the best baselines are within typical run-to-run noise. Baselines run at their papers' default settings.

claims.claim: The gains come at modest additional cost and time
claims.evidence: Table I: DeepSeek $0.073 vs $0.055 per instance (1.3x), 1,042 vs 815 s; GPT-5-mini $0.054 vs $0.024 (2.25x), 302 vs 187 s. Much cheaper than LingmaAgent ($0.155-0.309) and SWE-Debate ($0.382-0.738). A 2.25x cost increase on GPT-5-mini is not 'modest'.

claims.claim: The acquired QA knowledge is factually reliable (99.1% supported)
claims.evidence: §V-B1: 232 QA pairs stratified by outcome cell, each reviewed by two of four CS master's students, disagreements resolved by discussion. 42.2% fully accurate and 56.9% with minor errors (line numbers, function ownership). No agreement statistic.

claims.claim: Question decomposition and the category template are both essential
claims.evidence: Table II (DeepSeek only, single run): Proposal variant 66.0 (-4.8), free questions 67.0 (-3.8). The Proposal arm is a reasonable alternative and loses even to no pre-repair stage. The question-quality gap (Table III, +0.27 to +0.78 on a 10-point scale) is judged by DeepSeek-V3.2 on questions it generated.

claims.claim: QA injection shortens repair trajectories, mainly in locating and fixing
claims.evidence: §V-B2: mean rounds -7.1% over all 500 tasks and -17.1% on the 44 recovered tasks. Stage and QA-relatedness labels come from the authors' own annotation on that selected subset.

patterns.note: An explore-before-acting stage (targeted questions answered by read-only exploration) vs the same resolver without it: +3.8 and +4.4 pp on two models. It also beats a separate pre-pass that writes a single solution proposal (66.0 vs 70.8). This is agent-side discovery before a fix, not human pre-spec discovery. Single runs, Python only, and N=2 was picked on the test benchmark.

The read-only Answerer is a codebase QA agent required to cite files and symbols and to admit missing evidence. 99% of audited answers were supported, and injecting them beat both no QA and proposal-style output. The questions are generated by the agent, not by developers, and the Answerer design itself is not compared with alternatives.

Parallel, isolated, read-only Answerer sub-agents with a structured QA hand-off help. But the Proposal variant is also a separate read-only pre-pass and hurts, so the benefit lies in what is asked and handed back, not in isolation itself, which is never ablated. KB paper 2608.01507 found delegated sub-agent exploration lost on repository QA.

The questions are self-directed and answered by the repository, not by a human. The four-category template could inform what an agent asks a person before implementing, but there is no evidence here about asking people.

methodology.sample: SWE-bench Verified, 500 tasks (Python repos); motivating oracle experiment on 116 failed SWE-bench Lite tasks
methodology.baselines: Mini-SWE-Agent (same resolver, no pre-repair), LocAgent, CoSIL, LingmaAgent and SWE-Debate, all feeding Mini-SWE-Agent, at default settings from their papers
methodology.models: GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-V3.2; DeepSeek-V3.2 also as question-quality judge
methodology.variance: One run per configuration; Questioner at temperature 0.7; no seeds or confidence intervals
methodology.ablations: Proposal instead of QA; free-form questions; N = 0-3 (DeepSeek only)
methodology.contamination_controls: None. The question taxonomy was derived from oracle questions built with gold test patches on SWE-bench Lite, which comes from the same original test split as Verified and can share instances.

standards.artifacts: Code and data at github.com/LionLin2003/ACQUIRE; prompt templates in supplementary material

biases.detail: Single runs; the 1-2 pp margins over the best baselines and the ablation deltas have no intervals.
N=2 was chosen on SWE-bench Verified, and the category template was derived from SWE-bench Lite oracle cases that used gold patches.
Python repositories only; the authors flag other languages as future work.
Question quality was scored by DeepSeek-V3.2 on DeepSeek-generated questions, with no human check of the judge.
Trajectory-stage labels, QA-relatedness and the 'misleading QA' classification of regressions were all done by the authors' team.
SWE-bench Verified is public and predates both backbone models.

coi.affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; University of Pittsburgh; Guangdong Technion-Israel Institute of Technology
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None; GPT-5-mini and DeepSeek-V3.2 as backbones
coi.detail: Academic work. The SWE-Debate baseline shares authors with this paper, but it is a baseline that loses, so there is no favourable self-interest.

verdict_reason: The design is clean: the resolver is unchanged, so the gain is attributable to the injected QA, and the Proposal ablation is a meaningful alternative that loses. It uses two models, reports cost and time, human-audits the answers and releases code. But every result is a single run on one public Python benchmark, the margins over baselines are 1-3 pp, N and the question template were tuned on the same benchmark family, and question quality was judged by the generating model.
applicability: The most directly useful paper in this batch for the team's pre-spec discovery step. Before writing a spec or patch, have the agent write two targeted questions from the four categories: how does X behave, what contract does Y enforce, where does Z live and what depends on it, and what does the external standard or library require. Answer each in a separate read-only session that must cite files and symbols and must say when it cannot find evidence. The QA pairs become an inspectable artifact that a new developer can read and the spec can cite, which also serves onboarding and knowledge capture. Across 4+ Java repos, the 'locating and structure' and 'design and usage' categories matter most because of cross-repo contracts, but the paper covers only single-repo Python. Expect small gains and some regressions: 22 of 500 tasks got worse, 5 of them because the QA framed the wrong mechanism. Keep the QA as advisory context rather than instructions. Two questions beat three, so more context is not better. KB paper 2608.01507 found a delegating sub-agent design lost on repository QA, mostly at the hand-off, so the hand-off format (a structured question plus a cited answer) matters more than the decision to use sub-agents.

conflicts_with.detail: There, delegating grep/read exploration to a same-model sub-agent lost to a single vector-retrieval agent for every model on SWE-QA, with 41.8% of failures at the planner-to-sub-agent hand-off. Here, isolated read-only Answerer sub-agents whose structured QA is handed to the resolver improve repair by 3.8-4.4 pp. The task (QA accuracy vs repair), hand-off format and harness differ, and neither paper isolates sub-agent isolation itself.
